item.title: How to make more Charlie Kirks: Inside TPUSA's gap-year alternative to the 'college scam'
item.description: TPUSA's prep year program offers 18-year-olds the chance to delve into a classical, liberal arts education, with a focus on Great Books, as Charlie Kirk envisioned.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, aspiring young Americans have followed a predictable formula: high school, college, debt. But at the Turning Point USA prep year program, 18-year-old students are encouraged to pause, learn how to think, and discover their true purpose before committing to that considerable investment.

Dr. David Arnott, dean of the program, reflects on why the biggest problem in America isn't merely economics: it's character and wisdom. The mission is bold: use a year of classical, liberal arts education to mold the next generation of America's conservative leaders.

CHARLIE KIRK'S 10 MOST POWERFUL MOMENTS FROM COLLEGE CAMPUSES TO THE REPUBLICAN NATIONAL CONVENTION

Dr. Arnott sat down with Fox News at FreedomFest in Las Vegas to discuss how TPUSA's prep year is fulfilling Charlie Kirk's educational vision for America's youth:

"It is an ‘education about economics’ problem. I started my lecture here yesterday at FreedomFest asking the question, ‘why do we keep falling for socialism?’ And I tried to answer that question. And that's what I've been studying over the last 12 years as a Christian economist. 

"How do we distribute goods in a fallen world? And so I was asked by the people at Turning Point USA to be their dean of the prep year program in Fort Worth. Charlie Kirk's first book in 2022 was called ‘The College Scam.’ In 2026, he implemented his idea for education. 

"On September 2nd, the first class met in Fort Worth. He was assassinated eight days later on September 10th. What we're trying to do at prep year is to implement Charlie Kirk's idea for education."

Yet, Dr. Arnott emphasizes that the purpose of prep year is not to dissuade young people from pursuing a college education, but to ensure that they are prepared to do so if they make that choice.

"We're having this interview at FreedomFest. So I think people should have the freedom…they should have the freedom to go to college. They should have the freedom go into the trades. The problem is the government puts their thumb on the scale by supporting the price of college and, of course, forgiving the debt, which they shouldn't do anyway. If the government would just leave it alone, we'd be happy."

TPUSA's prep year program recently graduated its first class.

"We just dismissed our first class of 34, our inaugural class of prep year. It started September 2, 2025, and ended May 22, 2026. 34 students, about a third will be in college this fall. About a third will go into the trades. I just filled out an application the other day for one of the students to get a Mike Rowe Scholarship. And about a third will go on to other things that we don't know yet. 

"We are trying to implement what Charlie Kirk wanted. Which is the economic freedom to do with your life as you wish."

The launch of the program was immediately prior to Kirk's tragic assassination on the campus of Utah State University.

"He started [the program] on September 2nd, just eight days before he was assassinated, and so Charlie Kirk's ideas are really old ideas…they're not new, and so they encompass these things: Christian, liberal arts, classical and a Socratic teaching method. So that's what we do. We'll take in 35 to 50, maybe as many as 80 students in Elgin, Illinois and Fort Worth this fall. They'll be with us for nine months and we'll teach them those four ways of teaching.

"We'll teach them the disciplines of the Great Book, which is the Bible of course, great books by people like Dante and Virgil and Homer. We'll teach also how to get along in life, meaning how do you prepare yourself for life. And by the way…that's why we call it prep year. We're actually in the gap year industry. We take in 18-year-olds who have just graduated from high school. But we call it prep year because we are preparing them for life, more than just that education. 

CHARLIE KIRK SAYS 'UNDER NO CIRCUMSTANCE SHOULD A MAN EVER LET A WOMAN PAY FOR A DATE'

"And the real secret sauce that I can't explain to you because it's so hard to explain is the effect of being with 35 to 50 other committed Christian conservative 18-year-olds who are highly intelligent. The way in which they learn from each other and gain from each other is just spectacular."

As AI radically transforms education, learning, and the very face of knowledge itself, Arnott emphasizes that the program seeks to instill wisdom, not merely mastery of academic subjects:

"AI can't teach character, and that's what we teach at prep year and that is what Charlie Kirk wanted us to teach. He realized that there would be something coming along like AI that would answer all the technical questions of life, but it won't answer the important questions of life. 

"Wisdom is what we want these students to have. It's hard to teach wisdom, but that's what we're attempting to do. But as you said, David, that's why the traditional colleges have failed. They can teach people facts. They can't teach them wisdom. 

"If I had one sentence, a mission statement for prep year, it is to make more Charlie Kirks. And so my invitation to 18-year-olds just graduating from high school, you want to be more like Charlie Kirk? Come join us."

item.title: Days after Lindsay Clancy mistrial, another Massachusetts mom accused of killing her children seeks freedom
item.description: Janette MacAusland's defense sought dismissal after prosecutors said they still await the medical examiner's findings in the Wellesley murder case.
item.content:encoded:

Prosecutors told the court they are still awaiting the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner's official determination of the children's cause and manner of death, prompting defense attorney Joseph Krowski to ask that the case be dismissed or that Janette MacAusland be released on bail, WCVB reported.

A judge denied both requests, ordering MacAusland to remain held without bail.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Krowski and the Norfolk District Attorney's Office for comment.

MacAusland, 49, is charged with two counts of murder in the deaths of her 7-year-old son, Kai, and 6-year-old daughter, Ella, who were found dead inside the family's Wellesley home in April after police conducted a welfare check.

An arrest affidavit previously obtained by Fox News Digital alleges MacAusland confessed to killing the children after arriving at her aunt's home.

item.title: Donald Trump had no interest in watching the horrible NFL opener, ESPN's Taylor McGregor is a star & Danica!
item.description: First Thursday of football season kicks off with Aaron Rodgers torching Danica Patrick on Cam Heyward's podcast over their breakup and a Malibu house.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

First Thursday of football season. First real Thursday of football season. You know what that means, right?

Happy unofficial start to your weekend! Around here, weekends in the fall start on Thursdays — and for good reason.

We've got football all over the globe tonight. Obviously, the big one is the Rams-Niners in Melbourne, which technically takes place tomorrow morning at 10:30 a.m.

NFL PUSHES DEEPER INTO STREAMING AS NETFLIX LANDS AUSTRALIA GAME AMID FCC, DOJ SCRUTINY

We've also got a MASSIVE college game tonight. And by massive, I mean the point spread. No. 7 Miami is currently a 59.5 point favorite of FAMU. That has to be one of the largest point spreads I've ever seen.

It's on ACC Network, for those interested!

On that note, welcome to a Thursday Nightcaps — the one where Donald Trump was most certainly NOT interested in watching last night's football game.

Lordy. What a ballgame. Not a good ballgame, by any means, but a ballgame nonetheless.

What else? I've got Aaron Rodgers stuffing poor Danica Patrick in a locker, Boston radio stations are in absolute shambles today, and ESPN reporter Taylor McGregor continues to captivate America this week.

She was dominant during Monday night's power outage in Tallahassee, and she followed it up by arguing with a parking attendant during a radio interview earlier today.

What a week.

OK, let's get this thing going. Thursday night football is finally back. No time to waste.

Grab you a TV dinner for National TV Dinner Day, and settle in for a Thursday 'Cap!

Before we start ... man, do I miss TV dinners. The best. Obviously, I grew up in the 90s, so Kid Cuisine was my weapon of choice.

I feel like my mom fed me at least four of those a week. If I tried to even sneak one into my house nowadays for the kids, my wife would have me arrested.

MAHA moms are built different.

Hungry Man was great, too. That's the one that started it all, right? Those things weighed a literal ton out of the freezer. You could kill a man with one of those boxes.

But Lordy, they were good:

Amazing. What a commercial. They just don't make 'em like that anymore. Nowadays, it's all Big Pharma ads and insurance. We had it so good, and we just pissed it all away.

Sad.

Anyway, let's go ahead and get this class started with Donald Trump declaring last night's midterm party vs. NFL opener a triumphant SUCCESS!

"The Republican Midterm Convention last night, in Dallas, was a major, sold-out hit, far bigger, better, and more important than anyone thought possible," Trump said via Truth Social.

"It was really something, streaming all over the place, and really big numbers, despite going up against the NFL. The overall numbers beat the NFL. The Arena, which was really nice, beat its own attendance records. The place was packed! There were thousands of people outside who couldn’t get in. Screens were provided. I guess people LOVE TRUMP POLITICS! I’ll be there again tonight to close out the show."

Amazing. Between that declaration and the $5,000 we're all getting in a few months if we play ball, it was a great night!

Look, I have no clue if that's true. Did Trump's convention speech beat the NFL opener ... on NBC? I doubt it. I do know that those numbers aren't even out yet, so I'm not sure they're accurate regardless.

I will say ... he didn't miss much. What an awful game. A great game, because it's football, but a pretty horrible game for three quarters.

Drake Maye was a disaster. AJ Brown got hurt. Sam Darnold played five snaps and then missed the rest of the game.

Maybe stop shoving Pats-Seahawks down our throats, NFL? Ever think about that?

On that note, let's check in with Boston radio today as the Pats start the year 0-1:

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Football fans are the best. We wait nine months for our teams to play again. We suffer all winter long. We yearn for game days. We spend all summer counting down to kickoff.

And then, just like that, we're immediately pissed and want the whole thing blown up. It's like clockwork, every single year.

For what it's worth ... Maye was really, truly horrible last night. Just a baffling fourth quarter out of him, and I'm not even a big Maye fan.

Even I was stunned by this throw:

As a miserable Dolphins fan who had to suffer through Tua ... that fourth quarter gave me some pretty concerning flashbacks, Pats fans.

I'm just saying.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Thursday class into a big night of FOOTBALL. First up? A quick PSA for everyone that tonight's Rams-Niners game is on NETFLIX.

That's right. You're gonna have to subscribe to another streaming app to watch the second NFL game of the season:

Look, I think it's beyond dumb to put an NFL game behind a paywall. It's ridiculous, but that's the world we now live in.

I fear it ain't going anywhere, either.

That being said ... what an incredible promo by Netflix. Fair is fair, and I'm ready to run through a brick wall after that.

It also gives me the chance to bring Minka Kelly back to class. We simply can't have a Friday Night Lights-NFL promo and NOT check in with the star of that show:

Looks like she's doing well.

Clear eyes, full hearts, can't lose!

OK, two more on the way out. How about this humdinger from Aaron Rodgers about Danica Patrick on Cam Heyward's podcast this morning:

"I dated Danica. She had just retired. She was depressed and not fun to be around. But I didn’t leave her because I was trying to be there and be a good partner. Then it was going a certain direction, obviously. There was no intimacy; there was nothing," Rodgers said in the second part of the interview, which dropped Thursday morning.

"She tells a story that she was so blindsided and getting left by you, and that he leaves a trail of blood around him. And I’m like, what are you talking about? That’s not what happened."

Lordy. Rodgers, of course, wasn't done! Apparently, Danica tried to co-sign the mortgage with him on a new house in Malibu, and he wasn't having it.

"I’m buying a house in Malibu, and she goes, ‘Do you want to buy it together?’ And I said no. And she said, ‘You know what that means then?’ And I said, ‘Yeah, that’s the way things are going.’ She said, ‘Well, let’s get counseling.’ Then we got counseling. Then COVID hits and we’re stuck together."

My God. COVID was bad enough. Now you're putting Aaron Rodgers and an apparently "no fun" Danica Patrick in the same house together?

Sounds like a blast!

OK, that's it for today. Good work, everyone. Long class, but an important one.

Here's ESPN's newest star, Taylor McGregor, getting a parking ticket while doing a live radio hit.

See you tomorrow.

item.title: Trump defends $5,000 dividend proposal, praises 'beautiful' tariffs on 'Ingraham Angle'
item.description: President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend promise hinges on Republicans winning both the House and Senate in midterm elections, funded by tariff revenue.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump discussed his promise for economic payouts for every adult U.S. citizen in an interview with Fox News, promising that record trade revenue will build long-term national wealth.

Speaking on "The Ingraham Angle" in an interview airing before he closes out the first-ever Republican midterm convention Thursday, Trump discussed his promise to offer a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate. The president explained why the payments hinge on Republicans retaining control of both chambers.

"Because – they can't – I'll tell you what, because the Democrats can't do it," Trump told host Laura Ingraham. "Because with them, it's negative growth. with us, it's so positive."

"We're taking in $21 trillion. No country has ever taken in anywhere near that," the president added. "That's four-five times more than the next. That's all because of that beautiful word you and love more than most others – tariffs."

TUNE IN TO FOX NEWS TO SEE LAURA INGRAHAM'S INTERVIEW WITH PRESIDENT TRUMP AT 7PM ET ON ‘THE INGRAHAM ANGLE’

Trump’s offer came during the opening night of the Republican Party's midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, ahead of November's elections. Speaking to supporters, Trump detailed the proposal.

TRUMP MAKES STUNNING FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND CASH PROMISE IN BID TO RALLY GOP VOTERS AT DALLAS MIDTERM CONVENTION

"I can make this promise to you, and here is my promise," he said. "If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them, because of our economic — tremendous economic success like in history, we've never had anything like what's happening."

TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE

"But because of our tremendous strength and success economically — I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000. Very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders," Trump added.

The president said the dividend would have to be "spent in the U.S." Trump said tariff revenue would help fund payments to adult U.S. citizens if Republicans retained control of Congress. 

Republicans hold a narrow House majority with 218 seats to Democrats’ 214, with one independent and two vacancies.

WHITE HOUSE EXPOSES ‘TRANSSHIPMENT SCAM’ COSTING US UP TO $26B, POINTS FINGER AT CHINA

"So, we're taking in $21 trillion. Nobody – no country has ever taken in anywhere near that. It's four or five times higher than the next one," Trump said.

"All because of that beautiful word that you and I love more than most others: Tariffs," he added. While Trump pointed to tariffs to fund the initiative, annual tariff revenue falls well short of the proposal’s estimated cost.

GOP FACES BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS REPUBLICANS PAINT ELECTION AS ‘COMPETITION WITH COMMUNISM’

He opened the speech by discussing his performance since beginning his second term, saying he's "doing a great job." Trump quickly shifted to addressing the historical challenge that incumbent parties rarely retain control of Congress in midterm elections.

"But I say, why is it that, no matter how well you're doing, we see not a president — Democrat or Republican — almost never wins the midterms?" Trump said.

JOHNSON DOWNPLAYS GOP'S MIDTERM WOES AS DEMOCRATS EYE HOUSE TAKEOVER: 'I AM VERY BULLISH'

"We've got to change that because we have something going that's so good we can't let that string be broken. So, I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot, just one more time."

The payments could cost more than $1 trillion and add to the national debt. The proposal would also require congressional approval to be enacted. Some lawmakers have criticized the pledge as an attempt to buy votes, while Trump and his allies have compared the payments to corporate dividends.

The White House posted about the proposed payments in a statement Thursday, writing, "Last night, President Donald J. Trump unveiled the Trump Dividend — a historic $5,000 cash payment to every adult American citizen, made possible by the strength of the American economy under his leadership. The announcement is the latest proof that President Trump does what the so-called 'experts' say cannot be done: he delivers for the American people."

"The Trump Dividend depends on President Trump and Republicans. Democrat control means America loses — and working people pay the price," they added. 

Fox News Digital’s Peter D’Abrosca and Amanda Macias contributed to this report.

item.title: Pentagon witness blasts Virginia school district's 'vanilla' 9/11 teacher guide
item.description: Fairfax County, Va., schools face criticism over its new 9/11 guide, which identifies al Qaeda but emphasizes Muslim sensitivities and warns teachers not to “center the extremists."
item.content:encoded:
A wealthy Washington, D.C., suburb's public school district is advising teachers not to link 9/11 with radical Islam and to be sure to create "safe spaces" for Muslim students as the nation somberly marks the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks that killed nearly 3,000 Americans.

The guardrails in a six-page instructional guide, "25th Anniversary and Commemoration of 9/11" and distributed to teachers, has prompted critics to accuse Fairfax County (Virginia) Public School's liberal leaders of coddling post-9/11 sensitivities rather than teaching history.

s"It's sort of a vanilla way to do things," retired Navy Vice Admiral Lou Crenshaw, who was stationed inside the Pentagon when al Qaeda terrorists crashed a hijacked passenger jet into the building. "Everybody can go through the deal and feel good about it. And at the end of the day, nobody complains. 

CBC TELLS JOURNALISTS NOT TO CALL 9/11 ‘TERRORIST ATTACKS’ IN INTERNAL GUIDANCE

"To me, that's not exactly what we need to do. We need to make sure that the kids have learned a lesson here. And that's not going to happen if we try to shave the facts to the point where it's hard to figure out what we're talking about."

A digital content analysis reveals that about half of the 1,740-word document is devoted to tips for creating "safe spaces for Muslim and Middle Eastern students," about 15% spells out specific 9/11 instruction and the rest of the document tip-toes around managing "emotional responses" to the lesson.

The guide by the school district, which sits only a few miles from the Pentagon and several military bases, mentions military families only three times and first responders only once, saying at one point, "Many families of military personnel and first responders experienced loss and hardship."

Meanwhile, it has 30 references to Islam, "Muslim families," "Muslim students," "anti-Muslim racism," "anti-Middle Eastern" rhetoric, "Islamophobic rhetoric" and "Middle Eastern students" and families. It includes a bulleted list of "critical considerations" to challenge anti-Muslim bias.

The curriculum guidance speaks to a wider tension about how the 9/11 attacks are described by influential figures from teachers, journalists and politicians to social media influencers as a network of powerful Muslim organizations have built educational programs over the past 25 years downplaying discussions about the extremist interpretations of Islam that motivated al Qaeda and the 19 hijackers involved in the 9/11 attacks.

On Thursday, New York Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch called for "moral clarity" about what happened on 9/11, saying in a speech, "The men who attacked this city were terrorists. The men and women who ran into the towers to save innocent lives were heroes.

"Twenty-five years cannot be allowed to blur that distinction, and shame on those who do."

Last month, after a major public backlash, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reversed earlier guidance that instructed journalists to avoid calling 9/11 a "terrorist attack."

In a statement provided to Fox News Digital, Fairfax County Public Schools said the school community has a "deeply personal connection to September 11 because of our proximity to the Pentagon and the many military-connected families we serve.

"On the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks, we remember the nearly 3,000 people who were killed, including 184 at the Pentagon. We remember the victims, their families, the survivors, and everyone whose lives were forever changed. We honor the first responders whose courage and sacrifice continue to inspire us," the school district said.

"FCPS remains committed to creating an inclusive environment in our schools where all students feel welcome and respected as we strive to provide a world-class education and workplace."

LIZ PEEK: WE CANNOT LET THE LEFT REWRITE WHAT HAPPENED ON 9/11

Crenshaw saw the effects on military and civilian families impacted by the attack. On the fateful morning, Crenshaw was stationed on the Pentagon’s E Ring. He watched the TV footage of two airplanes crashing into the World Trade Center.

"I thought, 'This is not a good thing,'" Crenshaw recalled.

He then continued with a scheduled appointment, but as it began, the Pentagon was struck.

"Just about the time they sat down, and we started the interview, there was tremendous noise," Crenshaw said. "Bang! The entire building shook, and we knew right away that something bad had happened."

Crenshaw, who served in the Navy from 1974 to 2007, was on the fourth floor of the Pentagon on the same side of the building hit by the plane. His work area did not immediately collapse, although he said it was later destroyed by fire.

He looked outside and saw smoke billowing from the area where the airplane had hit. He also remembered seeing a chief petty officer crying as windows shattered and glass scattered across the floor.

The reality of the attack soon became clear to Crenshaw and the rest of the country. Al Qaeda, an extremist terrorist organization led by Usama bin Laden, had carried out a coordinated assault. The group used an extremist interpretation of Islam to justify the attack, portraying it as retaliation for the presence of U.S. forces overseas and American foreign policy. Bin Laden associate Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, who took credit for planning the attack, awaits a trial in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba.

Crenshaw said students should understand that 9/11 was not simply "a coordinated terrorist attack on the United States," as the FCPS script describes it, but a strategic act of war.

"What we saw in 9/11 was a religious extremist group, al Qaeda, who did not tolerate what the United States was doing around the world and decided to react violently," Crenshaw said.

Teachers should be prepared to discuss the Islamist extremism behind the attack without collectively blaming all Muslims, he said, noting that he agreed it is important to make sure Muslim students aren't shamed.

"They are a branch of Islam, but they certainly do not espouse any of the values that we know of Islam worldwide," said Crenshaw. "And, therefore, they really shouldn't be considered to be part of that mainstream religion."

The guide includes a section titled "Responding to Racism, Hate, and Bias against Muslims and Middle Eastern People," telling teachers that Muslim students experience "the worst anti-Muslim racism" during Sept. 11 lessons.

FCPS instructs teachers the anniversary "may intensify anti-Muslim and anti-Middle Eastern rhetoric." They are told that speaking out against anti-Muslim bias is part of their "sacred role as teachers."

The guide also says that if educators hear students or colleagues using "Islamophobic rhetoric," "it is up to you to disrupt."

Under a list of "Do" and "Don’t" instructions, FCPS explicitly tells teachers don't "associate the 9/11 attacks with Islam or Muslims" and don't "center the extremists or the acts of the extremists."

The guide says the commemoration should focus on "those whose lives were lost and those who sacrificed to help others – not those who attacked the United States."

The guide says teachers should not focus a commemorative lesson on "an examination of Islam." It argues that doing so could send the "harmful message" that "Islam, or all Muslims, are responsible for these terrorist attacks."

Crenshaw said not explaining the ideology of the hijackers and how al Qaeda interpreted Islam to justify the attacks means the guide fails to deliver "a sense of urgency or the evilness of what actually happened."

item.title: Iran-backed terror group’s latest territorial grab threatens second global shipping chokepoint
item.description: Iran-backed Houthi forces seized Yemen's Mocha port and advanced toward Bab el-Mandeb, threatening Red Sea shipping as Brent crude surged past $106.
item.content:encoded:
Iran-backed Houthi forces seized Yemen’s strategic port city of Mocha on Thursday and pushed toward positions overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, opening a potentially dangerous new front for global trade as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely constrained.

The advance threatens the southern gateway to the Red Sea just as Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on that route to bypass Hormuz — putting pressure on critical shipping lanes on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula and raising the risk of further disruptions to oil and commercial traffic through a key global trade choke point.

"Now you have Iran on one side of the Arabian Peninsula controlling Hormuz, and now the Houthis controlling Bab el-Mandeb on the other side of the peninsula," Hisham Al-Omeisy, senior Yemen advisor at the European Institute of Peace, told Fox News Digital. "Which basically is going to drive prices — oil prices, goods and everything else — up exponentially."

IRAN-BACKED TERROR PROXY HOUTHIS THREATEN FRESH ATTACKS AFTER YEMEN AIRPORT STRIKE

On background, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital: "The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges. We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability."

Yemeni government sources said Thursay the Houthis captured Mocha and reached the Hanish Islands, while Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces withdrew south toward Dhubab, which sits directly on the Bab el-Mandeb opposite the strategic island of Perim. Control of Dhubab and Perim would be critical to gaining a stronger hold over the strait, Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Sept. 10.

Bab el-Mandeb is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point and connects the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea and, farther north, the Suez Canal. It is a major artery for goods moving between Asia and Europe as well as energy shipments.

Its importance has grown dramatically during the Iran conflict.

WHO CONTROLS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ RIGHT NOW? HERE'S WHAT THE SHIP TRAFFIC ACTUALLY SHOWS

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported Sept. 9 that crude oil and petroleum liquids moving through Bab el-Mandeb averaged 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026, up from 5.4 million barrels per day in the final quarter of 2025. At the same time, flows through Hormuz plunged from 21.6 million barrels per day to just 4.9 million. The EIA attributed the increase at Bab el-Mandeb in part to Saudi Arabia rerouting crude through its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu to avoid Hormuz.

Al-Omeisy said the danger extends beyond the Houthis’ geographical gains. He said retreating government forces left behind military materiel that could strengthen Houthi forces on other fronts.

"People are focused on taking Mocha and those outposts on the Red Sea," Al-Omeisy said. "But the military side is terrible, particularly the equipment, the munitions, the vehicles, the drones that were at those military camps, which they can now, in turn, use against the government forces elsewhere."

RUBIO ACCU.S.ES IRAN OF FLYING IRGC PERSONNEL INTO YEMEN AS HOUTHI THREAT ESCALATES

Reuters separately reported Thursday that Iranian arms and direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards helped the Houthi advance, citing Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources. Two Iranian sources told Reuters that Tehran had instructed the Houthis to intensify attacks on Saudi Arabia and promised additional funding, weapons and senior officers. The seizure comes amid what conflict-monitoring organization ACLED described Sept. 9 as the most serious escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed camp since hostilities resumed in mid-July.

ACLED recorded at least 276 fatalities between Sept. 3 and 7 as clashes spread across al-Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwa, al-Jawf, al-Hudayda and Taizz, according to an analysis published Sept. 9.

Sherwan Hindreen Ali, ACLED’s Middle East research manager, said fighting along the Red Sea coast had become particularly intense as both sides sought control over territory with direct strategic importance to Bab el-Mandeb.

"Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in al-Hudaydah and Taizz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia/IRG have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab el-Mandab," Ali said in an analysis.

Saudi Arabia itself has also become more deeply involved.

EXPERT WARNS OF 'GENERAL ESCALATION' OF FIGHTING IF HOUTHIS RESUME RED SEA CAMPAIGN

Ali said Saudi forces launched at least 15 strikes against the Houthis between Sept. 3 and 7, mostly around Taizz, marking the highest number of Saudi strikes since Riyadh resumed military engagement against the Houthis in July.

The Houthis responded Sept. 8 with what Ali described as their largest wave of direct attacks on Saudi territory since March 2022, launching dozens of drones and ballistic missiles toward Abha, Jizan, Najran and Khamis Mushait. Ali said the attacks injured 73 people.

The widening fighting is now posing an early test for a new joint defense agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.

Al-Omeisy said the international response allowed the Houthis to exploit divisions among their opponents.

"The Houthis are also good in exploiting divisions and delays, they move rapidly on the ground to force a status quo while the international community debates merits, responsibilities and costs of an intervention."

The escalation also raises questions about Saudi Arabia’s newly signed defense agreement with Pakistan and Turkey.

IRAN-BACKED HOUTHI THREAT IN RED SEA COULD LEAD TO MAJOR US POLICY SHIFT, ANALYSTS SAY

The agreement, signed last month in Mecca, states that an armed attack against one member will be considered an attack against all three, Reuters reported Sept. 10. But after Houthi drones and ballistic missiles struck Saudi cities and energy infrastructure this week, Pakistan said Thursday that no military response under the pact was currently being discussed. 

"There is no such thing under discussion right now," Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said, according to Reuters. "When time comes [we] will act under the agreement." 

The Houthis, meanwhile, have said international navigation through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb remains safe, while maintaining that Saudi vessels are subject to their previously announced blockade, Reuters reported Thursday. 

Al-Omeisy warned that reversing the Houthis’ latest territorial gains could become increasingly difficult.

"The Houthis are really good at capturing a position, they entrench really well," he said. "They send these massive reinforcements, and then it’s going to be extremely difficult to push them out of those areas."

Oil markets were already responding to the widening regional threat Thursday. Brent crude jumped more than 5% to $106.60 a barrel by late Thursday morning, while U.S. crude climbed above $100 for the first time since May, according to Reuters.

item.title: Trump administration proposes ending 60-day grace period after job loss for H-1B, other visa holders
item.description: USCIS and DHS propose eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders who lose their jobs, requiring foreign workers to leave immediately.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) are preparing to propose a rule that would eliminate an existing grace period for visa holders who can't find a job, according to an unpublished document posted to the Federal Register.

Under current immigration laws, holders of certain visas, particularly H-1B visas, which are non-immigration visas that allow employers to sponsor skilled workers with Bachelor's degrees or higher, get a 60-day grace period to find a new job if they lose the employment tied to their visa.

The new rule proposal would eliminate that grace period, according to the document.

FEDERAL JUDGE STRIKES DOWN TRUMP’S $100K H-1B VISA FEE, RULING IT AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL TAX

"This proposal restores a direct relationship between an alien’s nonimmigrant status and the specific employment or activity that formed the basis of his or her admission or grant of status in the United States and reduces administrative burden," the document reads.

A noncitizen would have to immediately leave the U.S. if no longer working for an employer linked to a visa status if the rule were to be implemented.

US STATE DEPARTMENT HAS YANKED MORE THAN 175K VISAS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SO FAR

"DHS believes that restoring the expectation that aliens depart the United States upon cessation of the employment or activity upon which the alien’s status was based, would better promote program integrity and be more consistent with statutory purpose," the rule proposal reads.

The agency also claimed that eliminating the grace period would greatly reduce administrative burden "as the process of determining when the up to 60-day grace period may apply, reviewing the information submitted, and determining whether to shorten or eliminate the grace period may be time consuming and complex for the agency and confusing or unpredictable for the petitioner, alien and the alien’s dependents."

AMERICA’S BROKEN LEGAL IMMIGRATION SYSTEM IS REPLACING US WORKERS BY DESIGN

Before 2017, the document states, there was no 60-day grace period. But in 2016, DHS established the grace period in a rule that came into effec Jan. 17, 2017, three days before President Donald Trump first took office.

DHS also wrote that the rule's elimination would favor U.S. workers because employers who previously filled jobs with foreign workers would have less foreign-born labor to choose from.

"DHS assumes that almost all these entities would offer the same jobs to equally qualified U.S. workers, go through the I-129 petition process to sponsor nonimmigrant workers, or reassign the work to other current employees. DHS acknowledges that some of these petitioners may incur a temporary loss of productivity due to labor turnover," the rule proposal reads.

The unpublished rule is scheduled to publish Friday, Sept. 11, 2026, according to the Federal Register. It will then be subject to a two-month period of public comment before becoming law.

Fox News Digital contacted DHS and the White House for further comment.

item.title: What your HOA may be putting online about you
item.description: Homeowners association meeting minutes and membership lists can expose names, addresses and emails that scammers use to craft convincing phishing scams.
item.content:encoded:
A scammer doesn't need to hack your homeowners association. They may only need to look at information your community already makes available.

Meeting minutes, membership records and other association documents can contain details about the people who live in a community. Depending on the HOA and state law, some records may be available to association members while others could appear on an association website or another online system.

You probably didn't put the information there yourself. You may have no idea how much someone can learn about you. Yet a name tied to an address or community can give a scammer useful details for making a call or message sound legitimate.

What your HOA puts online could reveal more about you than you realize. Here's what to look for and what you can do about it.

THE ONE THING SCAMMERS CHECK BEFORE TARGETING YOU ONLINE

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

HOA records can contain details about homeowners, association business and community disputes. What members can access and what an association can publish depends heavily on state law.

HOA meeting minutes and other association records can reveal more than homeowners expect. How much information appears depends on the association and state law. Some states give HOA members broad rights to inspect association records. Sensitive disciplinary, collection and payment issues can receive additional privacy protections.

California provides a useful example. State law treats board meeting minutes as association records available for member inspection but excludes minutes and other information from executive sessions. Those closed sessions can cover matters such as member discipline, certain payment issues and other sensitive association business.

California law also allows an association to withhold or redact information when releasing it could reasonably lead to identity theft or fraud or compromise a member's privacy. The privacy concern grows when an association includes unnecessary personal details in records or makes information available more broadly than required.

HOA membership lists can contain information that scammers and data brokers would find useful. In California, state law defines the membership list as including a homeowner's name, property address, mailing address and email address as collected by the association. Members can request access to association records under state law.

Homeowners also have an important privacy option. California law allows members to opt out of sharing their name, property address, mailing address and email address through the membership list by notifying the association in writing. The law also restricts association records from being sold, used for commercial purposes or used for purposes unrelated to a member's interests as a member.

Rules differ from state to state, so check the laws where you live and ask your HOA exactly what information it collects, who can access it and whether you can opt out. The concern extends beyond the HOA itself. Once personal information appears publicly online, it can be indexed or copied and combined with information already collected from public records and other sources. Data brokers and people-search sites build profiles using many of those sources.

FIVE DATA BROKER OPT-OUT MYTHS THAT LEAVE RETIREES EXPOSED

Personal information gives scammers context they can use to make a fraudulent message feel legitimate. The Justice Department has already prosecuted companies that supplied consumer information to fraud operations.

Epsilon Data Management, one of the largest marketing companies in the country, agreed to pay $150 million after federal prosecutors said it sold consumer data to operators running fraudulent mass-mailing schemes involving fake sweepstakes and astrology solicitations. The government said many victims were elderly and vulnerable. A related company, Macromark, pleaded guilty after lists it provided to fraudulent clients resulted in at least $9.5 million in victim losses.

Those cases involved marketing databases rather than HOA records. Still, they demonstrate why personal details can become valuable to criminals. Names and addresses helped fraudsters identify and target potential victims.

HOA information can give scammers another source of context. A scammer who learns your name, street address and community can weave those details into a phone call, text or email. A message claiming to involve an assessment or another issue connected to your property can sound far more believable when the person contacting you already knows where you live.

Older adults remain especially attractive targets for financial scammers. The FBI says criminals may target older Americans because many have accumulated significant savings. Older victims can also be more likely to engage with unsolicited phone calls, texts or emails.

In 2025, Americans over 60 reported more than $7.7 billion in internet-enabled fraud losses. The FBI received more than 201,000 complaints from people in that age group, which reported the highest total losses of any age group.

Those numbers don't mean everyone living in a retirement or 55+ community will encounter fraud. They do show why reducing unnecessary personal information online deserves attention. The fewer details scammers can easily connect to you, the harder you make their job.

You may have more control over your HOA information than you realize, but your options depend on where you live and how your association handles its records.

Start by seeing what someone outside your community can find. Search your HOA's name along with terms such as "minutes," "directory," "membership list" or your own name. Check whether documents appear directly in search results without requiring a resident login. Pay particular attention to documents that connect your name with your address or other personal information.

Contact your board or management company and ask which records anyone on the internet can access. Find out which documents require a resident login and whether search engines can index anything posted on the association's website. If a document contains personal information that has no reason to appear publicly, ask whether the association can remove it, redact the information or restrict access.

Privacy rights vary by state, so find out what options apply where you live. California homeowners, for example, can opt out of sharing certain information through the HOA membership list. Other states may have different rules covering association directories and member records. Ask your HOA or management company how its opt-out process works and whether you can limit the contact information available to other members.

WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES

Even if your HOA removes information from a public page, your name, address and other details may already appear elsewhere online. People-search sites and data brokers gather personal information from public records, websites and other sources, then combine those details into profiles.

Start by searching for your name, phone number, email address and home address on major people-search sites. If you find a profile, look for the site's opt-out or removal process and submit a request to have your information deleted.

You can also use a data removal service to automate some of this work. These services send removal requests to data brokers on your behalf and may continue monitoring for information that reappears later.

Whichever route you choose, check back periodically. Personal information can resurface as data brokers refresh their databases or pull from new sources.

Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com

I doubt most HOA boards are thinking about scammers when they post meeting minutes or maintain a community directory. They are focused on running the neighborhood. The problem comes when information collected for one purpose becomes useful to someone with very different intentions. That is why I would spend a few minutes searching your HOA's name along with your own. See what a stranger can learn about you without logging in or proving they live in your community. You may be surprised by how quickly a name, home address and neighborhood can be connected. I would also ask your HOA what stays behind a resident login, what appears on the open web and what you can opt out of sharing. Laws vary by state, but there is no reason to make a scammer's research easier than it already is. And remember, removing something from an HOA website may only solve part of the problem. Once personal information spreads to people-search sites and data brokers, cutting down those profiles can help put some distance between you and anyone trying to build a convincing story around your life.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy fixation and alleged plot to poison husband emerge as accused mom claims psychosis
item.description: Corie A. Walsh's defense team claims a psychotic episode led to her son's death, but prosecutors allege she also had a plot to poison her husband.
item.content:encoded:
An Illinois mother accused of strangling her 2-year-old son was suffering a "psychotic episode" when the child was killed, her high-profile defense attorney says, even as prosecutors allege she was plotting to poison her husband.

The competing accounts come as Corie A. Walsh's attorneys accuse jail officials of failing to provide her prescribed psychiatric medication after hospital doctors recommended she receive around-the-clock psychiatric care upon her discharge, according to the defense.

The sharply different portrayals of Walsh's mental state underscore a central legal question likely to shape the case: whether evidence of severe mental illness can satisfy Illinois' legal standard for insanity.

ILLINOIS MOTHER CHARGED WITH MURDER IN DEATH OF 2-YEAR-OLD SON IN CASE DRAWING COMPARISONS TO LINDSAY CLANCY

Andrea Lyon, a prominent defense lawyer who previously served on Casey Anthony's legal team, said in a statement to Fox News Digital this week that Walsh's actions were driven by mental illness.

"This is a tragedy for the Walsh family, all of whom are mourning the loss of this child," Lyon said. "It is also a tragedy in that Corie herself was experiencing a psychotic episode at the time this happened."

MOM ‘VERY INVESTED’ IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE HIRES CASEY ANTHONY ATTORNEY AFTER ALLEGEDLY KILLING SON: DOCS

While Lyon described Walsh as experiencing a psychotic episode, legal experts say a psychiatric diagnosis alone does not determine whether someone meets Illinois' legal standard for insanity.

"The definition of insanity is, as a result of a mental defect or disability, that you're unable to appreciate the criminality of your conduct," Richard S. Kling, a clinical professor at Chicago-Kent College of Law and former Cook County public defender who has handled insanity cases, told Fox News Digital.

ACCUSED NC KILLER MOM PLANS INSANITY DEFENSE — AS RETIRED JUDGE SAYS MORE MAY FOLLOW LINDSAY CLANCY STRATEGY

Kling said psychiatrists first determine whether someone meets the criteria for a recognized mental illness before courts consider whether that illness prevented the person from appreciating the criminality of their conduct. He also said defendants who pursue an insanity defense must present evidence they were legally insane at the time of the alleged offense. Illinois also recognizes a separate verdict of guilty but mentally ill, distinct from a finding of not guilty by reason of insanity.

But behind the scenes, a battle over Walsh's mental health care is unfolding.

Following her arrest, Walsh was treated at Silver Cross Hospital for self-inflicted wounds to her wrists and thighs. According to her defense team, hospital doctors recommended she receive 24/7 psychiatric care upon her discharge.

However, Walsh's attorneys said she is not receiving her prescribed medication inside the Will County Adult Detention Facility.

The Will County Sheriff's Office, which oversees the jail, did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment regarding Walsh's medical treatment.

The defense's account differs sharply from prosecutors' allegations.

LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE SCORES ‘EXTREMELY HELPFUL’ PSYCHOSIS CONCESSION AS EXPERT FLAGS NEXT HURDLE

Along with three counts of first-degree murder, prosecutors also allege Walsh was planning to poison her husband Michael Walsh, before her son's death.

Further details regarding the alleged poisoning plot – including how far along the plan was or what substance was involved – were not immediately disclosed in court. Michael Walsh was traveling out of state when the couple's son was killed and flew home that evening. He has not responded to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Speaking generally and not about Corie Walsh's case specifically, Kling said evidence that a defendant planned or attempted to conceal a crime can become relevant in an insanity case because prosecutors may argue it shows the defendant understood the criminality of the conduct.

Walsh allegedly told police she killed the toddler because she believed he was the "devil," a petition seeking to deny her pretrial release states.

We all show our dedication and love in our own ways. As you probably are expecting, Machado Rivera told the deputies a completely different version of events. A version that doesn’t appear to include claims of an affair at all.

item.title: Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese show unity for Team USA at World Cup amid tense history
item.description: Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese connected repeatedly as Team USA set a Women's World Cup quarterfinal scoring record in a dominant win over Hungary.
item.content:encoded:
Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese had their best game together as teammates on Thursday in the quarterfinal round of the FIBA Women's World Cup against Hungary.

Their connection helped lead a historic 108-56 win for Team USA. It also gave fans another look at the growing partnership between two stars whose careers have been defined by competing against each other.

Clark and Reese repeatedly connected during the victory. Clark finished with 10 points, nine assists, three rebounds and two steals. Reese added nine points, six rebounds, three assists, two steals and a block.

Reese said their long history as opponents has made playing together easier.

"Yeah, I mean, we’ve played against each other so many times. So I’m sure we know each other’s game. Like the back of each other’s hand. So I just easily dished it off to her. She dished it off to me. She knows my slides. I kind of got one to her today or maybe two. So it’s fun. We just continue to build chemistry because we know we’re going to be USA teammates for a while," Reese said in an interview with TNT after the game.

CAITLIN CLARK AND ANGEL REESE MUST NOW WORK TOGETHER AT WOMEN'S WORLD CUP AS WNBA TAKES A HIGH-STAKES BREAK

Both players came off the bench again Thursday, but their shared minutes gave Team USA a combination it may rely on throughout the rest of the tournament. Clark creates scoring opportunities with her passing and outside shooting. Reese provides rebounding, physical defense and pressure around the basket.

While they were on the bench together, they were seen talking and laughing in a now-viral clip.

Their partnership has developed despite a history that has fueled one of the most intense debates in American sports.

The two stars first became permanently linked during the 2023 NCAA championship game. Reese led LSU to a 102-85 victory over Clark and Iowa before directing a "you can’t see me" gesture at Clark and pointing toward her ring finger late in the game.

The moment sparked a national argument about sportsmanship, race and perceived double standards. Clark had used a similar gesture earlier in the NCAA Tournament, and she later defended Reese against the criticism she received.

ANGEL REESE AND CAITLIN CLARK EXCHANGE WORDS IN SECOND DREAM-FEVER MEETING IN THREE DAYS

Their rematch in the 2024 Elite Eight became one of the most anticipated games in women’s college basketball history. Clark produced 41 points and 12 assists as Iowa defeated LSU 94–87. Reese finished with 17 points and 20 rebounds before fouling out.

The rivalry followed them into the WNBA after the Indiana Fever selected Clark first overall and the Chicago Sky drafted Reese seventh in 2024.

Clark ultimately won the league’s Rookie of the Year award. Reese led the WNBA in rebounding and joined Clark on the All-Rookie team. The constant comparisons between their performances kept the rivalry at the center of the league’s rapid rise in attention.

Their professional matchups also produced tense moments. Reese received a flagrant foul after striking Clark in the head during a 2024 game. In the opening game of the 2025 season, Clark received a flagrant foul for knocking Reese to the floor as Reese attempted to score. Reese quickly confronted Clark before teammates separated them.

Both players said the latter incident was simply a basketball play. They have also repeatedly rejected the suggestion that their competition amounts to a personal feud.

They previously showed they could play together during the 2024 WNBA All-Star Game. Clark assisted Reese on a layup as Team WNBA defeated the U.S. Olympic team. Clark finished with 10 assists, while Reese recorded 12 points and 11 rebounds.

THE PREDOMINANT BASKETBALL DYNASTY ON EARTH IS AT STAKE AS AMERICA'S EYES TURN TO CAITLIN CLARK'S ROLE

Their World Cup partnership carries significantly higher stakes.

Neither player made the American roster for the 2024 Paris Olympics. The World Cup represents their first senior international tournament and an opportunity to establish themselves as part of the program’s future before the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

Clark publicly praised Reese before the quarterfinal, calling her a fiery competitor with one of the strongest motors in the WNBA.

"We're both fiery, fiery competitors and we want to win and it's one of the things I really admire about [Reese's] game," Clark told the Associated Press. "She's competitive and she has a tremendous motor, like she has one of the best motors in the league. She works just as hard as anybody on the court. So, it's been fun to be able to play with her."

That competitive energy helped fuel a historic performance Thursday.

The Americans scored 36 points in the opening quarter and took a 59–30 advantage into halftime. Team USA shot 59% from the field and recorded 31 assists on 40 baskets. Its 108 points were the most ever scored in a Women’s World Cup quarterfinal.

The victory extended the United States’ World Cup winning streak to 34 games and moved the team within two victories of a fifth consecutive championship.

Team USA will face the winner of Australia and Spain in Saturday’s semifinal. Clark and Reese will enter that game with the same goal and, for one of the few times in their careers, the same fans behind them.

item.title: FBI arrests suspect accused of paying LA homeless to forge signatures using registered voters' identities
item.description: James Brass allegedly ran a ballot harvesting scheme on Los Angeles' Skid Row, paying homeless people to sign petitions using stolen voter identities.
item.content:encoded:
A California man was arrested early Thursday amid allegations that he and two others paid homeless people living in Los Angeles' Skid Row neighborhood to sign petitions using the stolen identities of registered voters in an effort to qualify ballot initiatives for local elections.

James Brass, 47, a.k.a. "Lord," was taken into federal custody in Victorville, 85 miles northeast of Los Angeles, the Justice Department said. Brass and the other two defendants — Courtney Price, 49, of Jacksonville, Florida, and Jateisha Herron, 33, of Boron, California — are charged with conspiracy to commit identity fraud in furtherance of a state felony.

Brass and Price are additionally charged with identity fraud in furtherance of a state felony.

TRUMP ELECTION FRAUD CRACKDOWN LANDS FIRST ARREST, PUTTING LONGTIME CRITICS IN WHITE HOUSE CROSSHAIRS

"Securing American elections from criminal interference is of the upmost importance to this FBI," FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital. "For at least 6 months in 2026, these subjects were allegedly paying homeless people on Skid Row in downtown Los Angeles to sign petitions in support of ballot initiatives, all using stolen identities of registered voters."

"Election security will always be a top priority of this FBI," Patel added. 

Brass allegedly orchestrated the ballot harvesting scheme through the management of a team of signature collectors, as well as collecting signatures himself, federal prosecutors said.

EX-NEW JERSEY MAYOR, HER HUSBAND CHARGED FOR USING FAKE BALLOT SIGNATURES AFTER SHE PLEADED GUILTY TO DUI

Price and Herron were employed by Brass, authorities said.

From February through August, the trio allegedly gathered the identities of voters from a database and handed the information to homeless people on Skid Row, a neighborhood in downtown Los Angeles that contains one of the largest concentrations of homeless people in the United States.

FORMER DEM MAYORAL CANDIDATE ADMITS FORGING VOTER REGISTRATION APPLICATIONS

FBI RAIDS SOROS-BACKED VOTER GROUP’S HEADQUARTERS IN REPORTED FRAUD PROBE

The homeless participants were allegedly paid to sign petitions in the names of the voters.

After the petitions were signed, Brass and Herron signed declarations at the bottom of the petitions, declaring that they personally witnessed the named registered voters sign the petitions and that each signature was, to the best of their knowledge, "the genuine signature of the person whose name it purports to be," federal prosecutors said.

The bogus petitions were turned in by Brass and Herron to petition coordinators. In total, authorities claim Brass was paid $41,600 from one petition management company.

Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said the alleged conduct "undermines the confidence voters have in our election systems," adding his office "will vigorously investigate and charge anyone involved in corrupting our elections."

All three defendants face up to five years in prison per count if convicted. Brass is expected to appear in court Thursday.

item.title: 20-year-old Michigan man killed by possible lightning strike in Florida
item.description: A witness described the powerful crack of lightning near the Disney College Program participant found unresponsive on a Celebration walking path.
item.content:encoded:
A 20-year-old Michigan man who had moved to Central Florida just days earlier to begin the Disney College Program was killed in an apparent lightning strike while on a walking path, authorities and his family said.

Matthew Eric Jenkins of Shelby Township, Michigan, was found unresponsive Tuesday evening on a walking path behind a hotel in Celebration, according to the Osceola County Sheriff's Office.

Jenkins' father told WESH-TV his son had moved to Central Florida last week to begin the internship program at Walt Disney World.

AMERICAN TOURIST KILLED BY LIGHTNING WHILE HIKING SICILY'S MOUNT ETNA

Deputies were called to the path in the 700 block of Bloom Street at about 6:25 p.m. Investigators said lightning had struck nearby.

Spyro Betz, who had been walking nearby before reaching his car, told FOX35 Orlando he heard a powerful crack of lightning.

"I heard the big crack of lightning that was like right overhead," Betz said.

He initially thought it had struck a building.

"When I heard the lightning strike, I expected it hit the building or something like that or hit the hotel. I didn't expect it to hit a person," Betz said.

Felipe Costa told WESH-TV he ran toward the path after hearing the lightning and found Jenkins on the ground.

LIGHTNING STRIKE TURNS 100-FOOT DINOSAUR INTO RAGING FIREBALL, STUNNING ONLOOKERS

"As soon as I heard that, I started running, and I came over here [where it happened]. That's when I saw the man," Costa said.

A woman joined Costa and began performing CPR while they waited for first responders.

Jenkins was taken to AdventHealth Celebration, where he was pronounced dead.

Jenkins' father told the outlet that the family was grateful to everyone who tried to help his son.

The sheriff's office said detectives are awaiting the medical examiner's determination of Jenkins' official cause of death.

item.title: Billy Joel says loud rock concerts damaged his nerves, led to his brain surgery and NPH diagnosis
item.description: Billy Joel revealed doctors told him playing rock 'n' roll music very loud was like a concussion every show, causing damage to his brain nerves.
item.content:encoded:
Billy Joel's love for the stage was also likely what lead to his brain disorder and subsequent surgery.

The "Uptown Girl" singer revealed his normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) diagnosis in May 2025. NPH affects his vision, hearing and balance, according to a statement Joel released on social media at the time.

Joel, 77, delved more into his recovery process during a recent appearance on his self-titled SiriusXM show, "The Billy Joel Channel" and said doctors told him that his rock 'n' roll lifestyle caused damage to his brain nerves.

BILLY JOEL SAYS AGING MUSICIANS WHO KEEP MAKING RECORDS PAST THEIR PRIME 'DILUTE THEIR LEGACY'

"I noticed that my balance was not good. I had this sense of being on a boat, like this rocking motion," Joel said of noticing initial issues. "I wasn't steady on my feet. I didn't know why that was, and I went to meet with the neurologist, and I was diagnosed with having something called normal pressure hydrocephalus, which they used to call water on the brain."

Doctors admitted NPH "could be progressive" and get worse and encouraged Joel to undergo surgery.

Joel remembered his medical team saying, "Well, we drill a hole through your skull, and we stick a shunt inside your brain."

CÉLINE DION REVEALS 17-YEAR SECRET HEALTH BATTLE BEFORE RARE DIAGNOSIS

"I didn't want to do that, but then I read up on it and I realized it can help improve your balance and can help your memory," he noted. "You know, I don't want to lose my marbles. It's hard to tell what's age and what's a condition, so I agreed to do the shunt and I had a surgery. And they implanted a shunt in my brain, and it actually improved things.

"My memory got better. My balance got a little better. My ability to function was better, and I realized, and the doctors told me this, because of my job, which is playing rock and roll music very loud, that it was giving me something like a concussion every time I did a show.

"It was causing damage to my brain nerves, and I could be losing more brain cells the more shows I did. And I realized that means I shouldn't be doing this right now. I got to improve."

Additionally, doctors didn't want the Piano Man to "stress too much," so he also began physical therapy while not performing.

"I'm doing whatever it is they tell me to do because I don't want to lose it, you know? So, I'm always testing myself," Joel said. "I know people have heard, 'Oh, he's got a brain disorder,' and I'm OK."

Joel added, "I just want people to know, don't worry about me. I'm not going anywhere. I'm here. I'm still here."

At the time of the announcement, Joel was forced to cancel a number of shows and said his condition had been "exacerbated by recent concert performances, leading to problems with hearing, vision and balance."

"Under his doctor’s instructions, Billy is undergoing specific physical therapy and has been advised to refrain from performing during this recovery period," his team said in a statement. "Billy is thankful for the excellent care he is receiving and is fully committed to prioritizing his health."

NPH is a condition that happens when cerebrospinal fluid builds up inside the skull and presses on the brain. This condition is most likely to occur in people over age 65. Treating this condition involves surgery to implant a shunt to drain excess fluid from the inside of the skull, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

During an appearance on Bill Maher's "Club Random" podcast last year, Joel said his balance has been most affected by the diagnosis.

"I feel fine. My balance sucks. It’s like being a boat," he told the former stand-up comedian. He noted that doctors have little understanding of the cause of NPH.
